grounding.audience: The published section is for business stakeholders. Write in business language: what people do, what the product does, what happens, and what is out of scope. Research catalogs and MCP tools internally; do not put catalog keys, tool names, graph identifiers, class or method names, matcher expressions, or resolution statistics in the published text. Those belong only in the lineage sidecar.
grounding.closed_names: Do not invent a product, role, function, or counterpart. Use only names and facts present in tool results and the shared briefs. Prefer canonical_names from system_brief.json, then names stakeholders would recognize (capability, actor, and process names) over internal module names.
grounding.one_story: A behaviour has one status for the whole document. Use status_ledger from system_brief.json. If the ledger or evidence shows it is incomplete, commented out, disabled, or not dispatched, it is not a live capability. Do not describe it as a working step, outcome, or interface in this section.
grounding.quote_conditions: When a rule has a number, status word, formula, or explicit condition, keep that wording in the business explanation. Do not invent a different threshold or rename a status.
grounding.scope_not_inventory: Tool results describe the operational landscape so you do not invent systems. They are not a table to dump into the document. If the landscape is broader than the specified capabilities and processes, say in plain language that those areas are not specified here.
grounding.do_not_universalize: Do not claim a control applies to every user, request, or path unless the records say so. Mention exceptions that appear in evidence, in business terms.
grounding.publish_structure: When process_flow records include flow_steps or alternate_paths, publish that structure as numbered steps with Goal, System Response, and Outcome per step, and quote user-visible denial text from alternate_paths. Do not flatten those records into a single narrative paragraph. A Mermaid diagram supplements the steps; it does not replace them.
grounding.publish_related: When a data entity and a constraint or rule describe the same fact, publish it on the entity and in the rules or validation section. Do not leave the fact only in lineage. Surface related config flags, related-party fields, and self-service variants instead of dropping them as too detailed.
grounding.verify_before_publishing: Each section's required_mcp is a mandatory floor (always mcm_get_domain_bundle): load every preferred_domain on each project before composing. Escalation tools when a claim is thin, ambiguous, or contradicted are optional depth, not a substitute for those bundle loads. Deeper evidence sharpens your conclusion; it does not enter the wording.

document_summary.heading: Document Summary
document_summary.query:
Write a Document Summary with two distinct sections:

FIRST SECTION - Document Metadata (do NOT include 'PART 1' or any section header in output):
Provide the following metadata fields with bold labels:
(1) System/Application Name. CRITICAL: Read `system_type` and `type_evidence` from architecture_brief.json. Put that type after the system name in parentheses. Format example: 'SystemName (VB6 Desktop Application for [brief description])'. Use `system_type` verbatim; do not inspect local file extensions such as .vbp, .frm, or .cls.
(2) Document Purpose (state it is a Business Functional Specification)
(3) Analysis Date
(4) Source of Analysis (e.g., reverse engineering from application source code, component documentation, assembly specifications)
(5) Scope Exclusions (state: excludes technical implementation details including programming languages, frameworks, database schemas, system architecture, performance metrics, infrastructure requirements, and deployment specifications)
(6) Intended Audience (list roles: business managers, product owners, business analysts, compliance officers, end users, stakeholders, operations staff)

Add a horizontal rule separator (---) after the metadata section.

SECOND SECTION - Executive Overview (add only '**Executive Overview**' as section header, do NOT include 'PART 2'):
Write a concise 3-4 sentence executive summary (target: 180-220 words maximum) for C-level stakeholders. Present as flowing prose covering: (1) primary business problem solved (one sentence), (2) top 3-4 capabilities in ONE sentence with inline comma-separated list (example format: 'Key capabilities include monitoring, tracking, reporting, and alerts'), (3) primary user types in ONE sentence with inline comma-separated list (example format: 'Primary users include managers, technicians, and administrators'), (4) top business value in ONE sentence focusing on 1-2 key benefits (example format: 'Delivers operational efficiency and regulatory compliance'). CRITICAL CONSTRAINTS: Use ONLY summary-level prose - NO bullet points, NO bold section labels like 'Key Capabilities:', NO detailed descriptions, NO multi-paragraph explanations. Total length MUST be under 220 words. This is a high-level executive briefing - avoid duplicating details that appear in subsequent document sections. Derive the system name from the catalogs and the system type from architecture_brief.json. Keep the executive overview at summary level and free of implementation vocabulary. Write for business stakeholders. Keep catalog keys, tool names, and implementation identifiers out of the published text; use them only while researching and put them in lineage. Invent nothing, and research as deeply as the evidence requires before publishing or dropping a claim. If evidence marks a behaviour incomplete or not executed, do not present it as working. If operations exist that are not specified, say so in plain language without listing internals.

Do NOT list business value or outcomes (those belong in Business Value section). Focus exclusively on problem context and scope boundaries - keep this to 2-3 concise paragraphs. FORMATTING: Use proper paragraph breaks. After every 2-3 sentences, start a new paragraph for readability. Describe what the product does and does not do; do not turn this into a module map. Write for business stakeholders. Keep catalog keys, tool names, and implementation identifiers out of the published text; use them only while researching and put them in lineage. IMPORTANT: Keep each value category concise - maximum 4-5 sentences per category. Focus on the most impactful benefits and use clear, direct language without excessive repetition.
